titulo: robos-impressos — print your pet robot’s body at home
meta: Three robot bodies to 3D print (dinosaur, capybara, and square robot), with room for servos, motors, Arduino, and Raspberry Pi. Parts generated by code and checked by a script. Phase 1: mechanics.
hero_chip: Robots to print at home · phase 1: the body · project not yet printed
hero_h1: Your pet robot starts with your 3D printer
hero_lead: You want a creature-like robot at home. Ready-made kits are expensive, and loose projects from the internet often don’t fit: hours of printing and filament wasted. robos-impressos provides the body: three models with a place for each motor and board, checked by a program before you print (you confirm the fit on your printer with a small test piece). Making it move on its own, with wiring and programming, comes in the next phase.
hero_alt: Illustration: a dinosaur, a capybara, and a toy square robot beside a 3D printer
resumo: You want to build a friendly robot at home and don’t know where to start with the body. robos-impressos is a set of three robot bodies to 3D print: a dinosaur and a capybara about 33 cm tall that roll across the floor, and a square desktop robot with a screen for a face. Each one already has the right space for the motors, servos (small motors that turn to an angle and stop), battery, and Arduino and Raspberry Pi boards. It’s for anyone with access to a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate who wants to build, learn, or teach robotics. This is phase 1, just the body and its fittings: wiring, voice, and intelligence are for phase 2. And an honest note: this is a digital project checked by a script; no one has printed these parts yet.
grade_alt: Illustration showing six steps: choose a model, print, fit the servos, assemble the shell, turn the head, ready for phase 2

prova_sub: A script (a small program) opens the print files, assembles the robot on the computer, and looks for problems. These are the numbers from the latest run, across all three models.
num1: parts to print, all closed and complete in the file
num2: parts intersecting one another, across all tested positions
num3: the thinnest wall measured in the shells (the target was at least 2 mm)
num4: is the largest part; the printer's build plate is 256 mm
barra_titulo: Estimated print hours per model (without a slicer: approximate only)
prova_ok_li:
• Each file is a closed solid made of a single body.
  • Every part fits on the 256 × 256 × 256 mm build plate.
  • No part occupies the space of another part or a component (servo, motor, board, battery), with the head, mouth, and arms at the extremes.
  • Every part can reach its position: the script brings them in one at a time, in assembly order, and flags any collision with what is already assembled.
  • No part is floating in the air, and the center of gravity falls inside the supports, with clearance.
  • The test itself is tested: one part is deliberately moved 3 mm, and the script must flag it.
prova_nao_t: What only printing can tell you
prova_nao_li:
• No one has printed or assembled these parts yet.
  • Print time and filament use are volume-based estimates.
  • Some component dimensions have no official source (servo tabs, motor driver holes). They are marked NC in cad/parametros.py and section 4 of PLANO.md (in Portuguese): measure your part with calipers and, if it differs, change the number and generate the parts again.
  • The script does not test strength, whether a screwdriver can reach every screw, or the 3 mm fit of the servos in the arms and mouth.
plano_h2: From file to assembled robot body
plano_sub: Five steps, no programming needed. At the end, you have the assembled body, with servos and motors in place; making it move is phase 2.
pl1_p: The square robot has fewer parts (14), but needs a Raspberry Pi and screen. The dinosaur and capybara each have about 38 parts, and you can swap one shell for the other later.
pl2_p: One pack of M3 threaded inserts, some M3 screws, and a soldering iron are enough for the test; for the animals, you also need a micro servo (the square robot does not use one). The rest (servos, wheel motors, battery holder, switch) are common parts at electronics shops in Brazil. The servos and motors are only for checking the fit at this stage: they will not move yet.
pl3_p: It’s a 7 cm test plate that checks the fit of the micro servo, inserts, screws, and guide pin on your printer. Less than an hour of printing can save you from redoing a five-hour part. If everything fits, you can continue without installing anything.
pl4_p: The parts come laid out in the right orientation and separated by color. The skeleton is printed in PETG, which is more durable; the shell in PLA.
pl5_p: First the skeleton with motors and servos, then the shell, and finally the head. The order, screw by screw, is in the project plan.

p2_p: cad/verificar.py reads the exported STL files and rejects open parts, oversized parts, thin walls, parts intersecting each other, parts that cannot reach their position, and robots that tip over.
p3_p: The chassis, trays, fork, and neck cradle use the same files for the dinosaur and the capybara (pecas/comum/).
fluxo_sub: The animals’ outer shells are made by adding rounded shapes together and turning them into a mesh; holes, pockets, and cuts are exact operations applied on top.

fx2_p: Assembles the robot from the files, moves the joints to their limits, measures overlaps by shared volume, and rebuilds the assembly one part at a time.
fx3_p: Blender produces the images on this page: assembled, exploded, skeleton, and build plates.
pre_sub: To just print, all you need is a printer, a slicer, and the ZIP download. Python and Blender are for anyone who wants to change the project.
pre1_p: A printer with a 256 mm build plate (the project was designed for the Bambu Lab A1; it does not fit on a 220 mm plate because the largest part is 226 mm), PLA and PETG filament, a slicer such as Bambu Studio, and the components on the shopping list.
pre2_p: Python 3.12 or later (download it from python.org; the library versions require it) and git. The libraries are installed in an isolated environment inside the folder.

guia_sub: These are the repository commands. The complete assembly sequence, with every screw, is in PLANO.md (in Portuguese).
g1_p: The print files are ready in the pecas/ folder, in STL and 3MF formats. If you only want to print, download the ZIP (about 80 MB), extract it, and open the files in your slicer: you do not need a terminal or Python. The componentes/ folders are only outlines of purchased parts: do not print them.
g2_p: Print the test piece and a guide pin (pecas/comum/stl/comum-pino-guia.stl). The drawing below shows each hole from above. Beside the micro servo window are three insert holes (3,9, 4,0 and 4,1 mm), and at the tip is the larger hole for the yellow motor shaft (the shaft must turn freely). The other row has three guide-pin sockets (clearances of 0,20, 0,25 and 0,30 mm) and four screw holes: M3 that passes freely, M3 that threads into the plastic (M3* in the drawing), M2,5 and M2. The design uses the 4,0 mm hole and the 0,25 mm socket, the middle ones, marked with a dimple (● in the drawing). The M3 insert (the brass sleeve that goes in hot, with a soldering iron, and provides threads) must fit snugly; the pin must fit firmly without hammering. If both fit, continue. If a neighboring size fits better, adjust the clearance in cad/parametros.py, in the FOLGA block (componente for the servo, encaixe for the pin, inserto_d for the insert), and regenerate from step 3: that’s the only time you need Python.
g2_c: open this file in the slicer
g3_t: Generate and check (only if you changed a measurement)
g3_p: The first command recreates all the parts; the second runs the 9 tests and exits with an error if any fail.
g4_p: Each build plate below is one print: the parts are already laid flat, grouped by color and material, in a 3MF file with the geometry (the file doesn’t include slicer settings and hasn’t been opened in a slicer yet; if yours won’t open it, use the individual STL files in pecas/<modelo>/stl and the table). The filename is <modelo>-mesa-NN-material-cor.3mf. Untested starting point: 0,2 mm layer height, 0,4 mm nozzle, 3 walls and 15 % infill. The rounded shells need tree supports; the skeleton prints without supports, except for berco-tilt. The test piece and guide pins are repeated on the gray build plate: if you’ve already printed them, remove them from the plate. Colors are just for appearance: the minimum is one roll of PETG for the skeleton and one of PLA for the shell. In the tables, mesa-cabeca is the name of a part (the one that supports the head from the inside).

g5_p: Assembly order for the dinosaur and capybara:
g5_li:
• Heat-set the M3 threaded inserts into the parts.
  • Screw the two motors onto the chassis walls (the large dark part, which is the skeleton), from the outside, with the motor facing up.
  • Attach the support ball with its cover underneath.
  • Mount the head-turning servo on top of the chassis, then the fork, the second servo, and the cradle (the two neck parts).
  • Put the battery and board trays in from the back.
  • Close the torso from the front, then fit the wheels from the sides.
  • Belly panel, back, legs or thighs, tail.
  • Assemble the head on the workbench (the mesa-cabeca part goes under the skull; then add the mouth servo, jaw, and eyes) and lower the whole head onto the neck: two screws from above, hidden under the crest.
  • Spikes, claws, ears, and bandana are press-fit or glued in place.
g6_li:
• Servo on the base floor and Arduino beside it; then the large gear on top of the servo.
  • Insert the battery through the rear door.
  • Neck tube under the cover, then the cover on the base.
  • Fork on top of the tube, with three long screws.
  • Raspberry Pi, screen, and the second servo on the head frame.
  • Head shell from the rear, screen frame from the front.
  • Head between the fork arms and the rear door.
cp_3: Yellow 1:48 TT motor with 65 mm wheel
cp_8: 3.5-inch screen for Raspberry Pi, model MPI3501 (fits the board pins; an HDMI screen will not work)
cp_11: M3 screws, nuts, and washers (and a few M2.5)
compras_nota: In phase 1, nothing is connected: Arduino and Raspberry Pi are only used to check the fit, so they’re optional (in the square robot, the Raspberry Pi holds the screen). Screws outside the common kit: for the creatures, 2 M3×12 flat-head and 4 M2,5×8; for the square robot, 3 M3×35, 8 M3×12 flat-head and 4 M2,5×12. The full list is in PLANO.md (in Portuguese), section 3, and the quantities for each stage are in section 6.

ferramentas: Tools: soldering iron (for the inserts), small Phillips screwdriver, 2.5 mm Allen key, calipers (to measure your components), and instant glue.
pilhas_nota: Be careful with 18650 batteries: they are lithium batteries. Use a proper holder and charger, keep the terminals from touching metal, and don't charge them unattended, especially with children nearby.

pal_h2: If any of these names are new to you
pal_dl: <dt>Servo</dt><dd>A small motor that turns to an angle and stops there. It turns the head and opens the mouth.</dd><dt>Arduino and Raspberry Pi</dt><dd>Two electronic boards. Arduino controls motors and servos; Raspberry Pi is a small computer that handles voice and camera in phase 2.</dd><dt>Script</dt><dd>A small program. Here, it generates the parts and checks that they’re correct.</dd><dt>Render</dt><dd>An image made on a computer from the 3D file. It isn’t a photo.</dd><dt>PLA and PETG</dt><dd>Two printing plastics. PLA gives a nice finish; PETG handles more force and heat.</dd><dt>Build plate</dt><dd>The printer’s base. “12 build plates” means 12 prints, one after another.</dd><dt>M3 insert</dt><dd>A threaded brass sleeve that goes into the plastic while hot so the 3 mm screw holds firmly.</dd><dt>18650 battery</dt><dd>A rechargeable lithium battery, a little larger than a regular battery.</dd><dt>Motor driver</dt><dd>A small board that lets Arduino start and reverse the wheel motors.</dd><dt>TT motor</dt><dd>The small yellow geared motor commonly used in robotics cars.</dd><dt>Shield</dt><dd>A board that fits on top of Arduino to make connecting the servos easier.</dd><dt>Rocker switch</dt><dd>The on/off switch.</dd><dt>Chassis, fork and cradle</dt><dd>Skeleton parts: the chassis is the base with the walls; the fork and cradle are the two neck parts.</dd><dt>Pan, tilt, horn and CG</dt><dd>Terms in the checker output: pan means turning side to side; tilt means angling up and down; horn is the small part attached to the servo shaft; CG is the center of gravity.</dd><dt>Guide pin</dt><dd>A printed 4 mm pin that aligns the front and back halves of the torso. The hole it goes into is the socket.</dd><dt>NC</dt><dd>Not confirmed: a component measurement without an official source that you check on your own part.</dd>
